reading.rtitle: What the Headline Figure Does Not Say
paras: Revenue at the company rose by 18 percent last year, from 410 million reais to just under 485 million. That is the headline figure, and it is the one that appeared in every newspaper that covered the results. It is also the least interesting number in the report. Revenue in residential construction follows the market, and the market in the state grew by almost exactly the same amount. In other words, the company did what the market did.

The numbers that say something are further down. The backlog, the value of contracts that have been signed but not built yet, soared to well over 900 million reais, the highest in the company’s history. At the same time, the average cost overrun on finished projects fell from 11 percent to 4 percent. The company is not only selling more; it is also delivering what it sells much closer to the budget. Margins, which had plummeted during the downturn of 2016, peaked in 2023 and have leveled off since then at around 9 percent.

Numbers like these only mean something when you put them into perspective. A backlog of 900 million sounds large until you know that it represents about two years of work at the current pace. An overrun of 4 percent sounds small until you remember that the industry average is in the region of 15 percent. A good report, like a good interview answer, does not give you more numbers. It gives you fewer, and it tells you what each one is being compared with.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 text, written for this lesson from the structure of published annual reports of listed Brazilian builders

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: The company had its best year ever because revenue rose faster than the market.
The headline revenue figure says less than the backlog and the cost overruns, and every number needs a comparison to mean something.
Annual reports give too few numbers, so readers cannot judge a company properly.

listenings.text: Numbers are where most candidates lose me, and they lose me in one of two ways. Some give me no numbers at all. They tell me the company grew a lot, and I have no idea whether a lot means ten percent or ten times. Others give me so many numbers that I stop listening after the third one. Here is what works. Give me one headline figure, and round it. Nobody needs to hear four hundred and eighty-four point six million. Just under four hundred and eighty-five million is perfect, and so is almost half a billion. Then give me one comparison, so that I know whether the number is big or small. And then stop. If I want the breakdown, I will ask for it. The candidates I remember are not the ones with the most numbers. They are the ones who told me what one number meant.

The worst number I ever had to present was a cost overrun of twenty-two percent on a hospital project. The board saw that figure on the first slide, and the room went quiet. I had two choices. I could hide it in the breakdown, or I could put it into perspective. I chose the second. I explained that almost three quarters of the overrun came from one decision, a change in the ventilation system that the client asked for after the pandemic. Without that change, the overrun was in the region of six percent, well under the industry average. Then I showed them the trend. Overruns on our projects had peaked three years earlier and had been falling steadily since then. The board approved the next project that same afternoon. The number did not change. What changed was the comparison they had in their heads.
